`openos`: run an OpenComputers program.

## Synopsis

<strong>openos</strong> <em>program</em> \[<em>args</em>\]

## Description

<strong>openos</strong> runs a program written for OpenComputers' OpenOS on mcos, as wine runs a Windows program on Linux: in a machine of its own, with OpenComputers' <strong>component</strong>, <strong>computer</strong> and <strong>unicode</strong> libraries, and OpenOS's own libraries (event, term, keyboard, shell, filesystem, serialization, text, sides, colors, uuid, robot), ported. <em>program</em> is a path, with or without its <strong>.lua</strong>.

The gpu draws on the program's terminal (its screen, a tier's colors and size), and the keyboard and mouse are the terminal's (key\_down, key\_up, touch, drag, drop, scroll, clipboard). Devices are components by an adapter: the EEPROM (eeprom), a redstone card (redstone), a network card (modem, over UDP), a golem's robotics (robot). Other devices aren't components. Ctrl+C is OpenOS's: an interrupted signal; Ctrl+Alt+C ends the program.

Whatever OpenOS had that <strong>openos</strong> doesn't is an error saying so, never something else done instead: a library (process, thread, internet...), a method (a gpu's video memory, a robot's tanks).

## Exit status

What the program's <strong>os.exit</strong> gave, or the integer it returned; 0 when it ends; 1 when it fails, its error on standard error; 127 when the program isn't there.

## Notes

mcos's commands run where OpenOS's would: <strong>os.execute</strong> and <strong>shell.execute</strong> run mcos's <strong>sh</strong>. A modem message of one string is that string, so mcos programs (nc -u) talk with it. A golem's inventory is its hand, one slot. A redstone face's input is its level, the card's own output included.
